title: Financial Literacy for Teens
summary: Money skills for young people: needs and wants, making a budget with 50/30/20, saving and goals including community savings groups, compound interest, borrowing and the cost of debt, banking, mobile money, scams and gambling, and earning and investing. Calculations were checked in code.
audience: Teenagers, secondary school students and the parents and teachers who support them

body.p: Financial literacy means understanding how to earn, spend, save, borrow and protect money. Learning it as a teenager gives you a huge advantage: good habits started early grow over a lifetime, and mistakes are smaller and easier to fix while you are young.

list: Needs are things you must have: food, shelter, basic clothing, school costs and transport.
Wants are things that are nice to have: the latest phone, takeaways, branded shoes or extra data for streaming.
Many items have a need part and a want part: you may need shoes, but want a particular brand.

body.p: Teenagers may receive pocket money or gifts, or earn from part-time work, tutoring, selling crafts or snacks, or helping neighbours. Earning your own money teaches its value: if you earn R20 an hour, a R300 item costs you 15 hours of work.

body.tip: Before buying something, ask: is this a need or a want, and how many hours of work does it cost?

body.p: A budget is a plan for your money. It helps you control spending, avoid running out and reach goals.

One simple guide splits money into 50% for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for saving. With R500 a month, that is R250 for needs (such as transport and school items), R150 for wants and R100 for savings. Adjust the proportions to your situation; the key is to decide in advance.

steps: Write down all the money you expect to receive.
List what you need to pay for.
Decide how much to save first, before spending.
Track what you actually spend for a month, in a notebook or app.

body.p: Buying a R20 snack three times a week costs 3 x 20 x 4 = R240 a month, or R2880 a year. Spotting these leaks is one of the easiest ways to free money for goals.

body.tip: Pay yourself first: move savings aside as soon as you receive money, not at the end of the month.

body.p: Saving means keeping some money for later. It gives you security for emergencies and lets you reach goals without borrowing.

list: Short-term goals: a new pair of shoes or a school trip.
Medium-term goals: a laptop or course fees.
Long-term goals: further education, starting a business or a home.

body.p: Saving R50 every week adds up to 50 x 52 = R2600 in a year. Write the goal down, decide the weekly amount and track progress; seeing it grow keeps you motivated.

list: A youth or student savings account at a bank, often with no or low fees.
Mobile money savings features.

Community savings groups such as stokvels, chamas, tontines and susu, where members contribute regularly and take turns receiving the pot or share savings and interest. Choose well-run groups with clear rules and records.

body.tip: Keep emergency savings separate from goal savings, so an emergency does not wipe out your plans.

body.p: When you save or invest, interest is paid on your money, and then on the interest too. R1000 at 10% a year becomes R1100 after one year, R1210 after two and R1331 after three. The earlier you start, the more time compounding has to work.

Borrowing means using someone else's money now and paying back more later. Compounding works against you with debt. A loan of R1000 at 20% interest a month becomes R1200 after one month and, if not repaid, about R2073.60 after four months, more than double. Informal lenders (loan sharks) and some instant digital loans can charge extremely high rates and use harsh collection methods.

list: Borrow only for things that improve your future, such as education, and only what you can repay.
Read the terms: interest rate, fees, repayment dates and penalties.
Avoid borrowing for wants, such as clothes or betting.
Your repayment record affects your credit score, which decides whether you can borrow later.

body.tip: If you must borrow, compare the total amount you will repay, not just the monthly payment.

lessons.title: Banking, mobile money and staying safe

list: Bank accounts keep money safer than cash and let you receive payments and build a financial record.
Mobile money services such as M-Pesa, MTN MoMo and Airtel Money let you send, receive, save and pay using a phone; check transaction fees, as frequent small transfers add up.
Debit cards spend your own money; credit cards and buy-now-pay-later services are forms of borrowing.
Keep your PIN secret, and never write it on your card or share it, even with friends.

body.p: Scammers target young people with fake prizes, "investment" schemes promising huge returns, fake job offers and messages asking for PINs or one-time passwords. If it sounds too good to be true, it is. No genuine bank or mobile money provider will ask for your PIN. Sports betting and gambling apps are designed so that most players lose money over time; many countries ban gambling under age 18.
Pyramid and Ponzi schemes pay early members with money from new members and always collapse, leaving most people with losses.

body.tip: Pause before any money decision someone pressures you to make quickly; urgency is a classic scam tactic.

list: Build skills that people pay for, such as digital skills, languages, trades, tutoring and creative work.
Start a small side business: identify a need, keep costs low, record sales and expenses, and reinvest profits.
Understand payslips: gross pay, deductions such as tax and pension contributions, and net pay.

body.p: Investing means putting money into assets that may grow, such as shares, unit trusts or government bonds. Higher potential returns come with higher risk, and investments can fall in value. Diversify (do not put all your money in one place), invest for the long term, and only invest through regulated providers.

Write down one savings goal, a monthly budget and one skill you will build to earn more. Review it every few months. If you save 15% of everything you earn from your first job onwards, you will be ahead of most adults.

body.tip: Talk openly about money with family and trusted adults; it is a skill, not a secret.

quiz.q: Earning R20 an hour, a R300 item costs:

options: Spend first and save what's left
Save as soon as you receive money

quiz.q: A R20 snack three times a week costs about how much a year?
Saving R50 a week for a year gives:
R1000 at 10% a year compounded for three years becomes:
R1000 at 20% a month unpaid for four months grows to about:

options: The total amount you will repay

quiz.q: A genuine bank or mobile money provider will:
options: Ask for your PIN by SMS
Ask for your PIN by phone
Always collapse, leaving most people with losses
Not putting all your money in one place

quiz.q: Higher potential investment returns usually come with:
